desc: Derive the feasibility check precisely: "can achieve shortest distance ≥ D using ≤ K chosen edges" reduces to min-cut on layered graph (layers 0..D-1), where each original edge gives a capacity-1 "unchosen" arc (u,i)→(v,i) and ∞ "chosen" arc (u,i)→(v,i+1); min cut = min edges to choose.

Implement Dinic max-flow and ok(D): nodes (v,c) for c in 0..D-1, source (1,0), sink T with ∞ arcs from (N,c); per edge (u,v): capacity-1 arc (u,c)→(v,c), ∞ arc (u,c)→(v,c+1) if c+1<D; feasible iff maxflow ≤ K. D=0 trivially feasible.
Implement binary search over D in [0, M] (safe upper bound; distance ≤ shortest path length ≤ N-1 anyway, but M is safe).

Build brute-force solver (enumerate all C(M,K) subsets, BFS/0-1 BFS for shortest path) for tiny graphs and cross-validate the flow solution on many random small cases (N ≤ 6, M ≤ 8, all K in 1..M), including multi-edges and graphs with direct 1→N edges — several thousand instances, zero mismatches.
Test against samples: expect 1, 2, 0 (sample 3 checks multi-edge handling) — all pass.
Double-counting concern (same edge cut across layers) resolved: min-cut equals min number of original edges; confirmed empirically by brute force.
Confirm edge cases: K=M, D=0, unreachable intermediate vertices, answer 0 cases; complexity fine (≤3001 nodes, ~20k arcs, ~7 flow runs).
Final Python solution written: reads stdin, prints answer, Dinic implementation, correct on samples and brute-force cross-validation.
